modules.title: Clean and prepare data
modules.summary: Turn messy, real-world data into a tidy table you can trust, using text, date and number functions, and the habits of Power Query.
modules.outcome: You can clean names, numbers stored as text and dates with formulas, spot a table that is not tidy, and record each cleaning step so it can be repeated.
modules.intro: Analysts say that most of the work in data analysis is preparing the data, and they are right. Exports arrive with extra spaces, numbers typed as text, dates in three formats and blank rows. Before any chart or average means anything, the data has to be tidy. This module teaches the cleaning formulas, the idea of tidy data, and the discipline professionals use: change a copy, never the original, and write down every step so you can do it again next month. You practise the formulas in the in-browser sheet; the lessons also show where the same steps live in Excel's Power Query, which runs on the desktop.

topics.title: Tidy data: the shape analysis needs
topics.html:
Almost every tool for analysis (pivot tables, charts, SQL, Power BI) expects the same shape, called tidy data: each column is one variable (a fact such as date, region or amount), each row is one observation (one order, one visit), and each table holds one kind of thing. If your data is in a different shape, the first job is to reshape it, not to work around it.

A common untidy layout and its tidy version
Untidy (one column per month)Tidy (one row per product and month)
Product | Jan | Feb | MarProduct | Month | Sales
Pen | 100 | 120 | 90Pen | Jan | 100
Book | 80 | 95 | 110Pen | Feb | 120 · Pen | Mar | 90 · Book | Jan | 80 …

The untidy version is fine for a person to read. But the month is hidden in the column names, so you cannot filter by month, group by month or chart months without special effort. In the tidy version, month is a column like any other. Excel's Power Query has a command for this exact change, called Unpivot Columns.

Signs that a table is not tidy

  • Months, years or categories are used as column headings.
  • Merged cells, or headings that span several columns.
  • Blank rows or columns that split the data, or totals typed into the middle of it.
  • Several facts squeezed into one cell (Pune, 411001).
  • Numbers stored as text (Rs 1,200), or dates as text.
  • The same thing spelled several ways (Delhi, New Delhi, delhi ).
Watch out

Keep the raw data untouched. Put your cleaned version on a new sheet or in new columns beside it. If a cleaning rule turns out to be wrong, you can go back and redo it; if you overwrote the original, you cannot.

Worked example

Is this tidy?

A sheet has columns: Date, Region, Product, Units, Revenue, and a final row 'Total' with the sums.

  1. Each column is one fact: yes.
  2. Each row is one sale: yes, apart from the last row.
  3. The Total row is not an observation. It breaks pivots and averages.

Answer. Almost tidy. Remove the Total row from the data (calculate totals in a separate cell or a pivot) and it is ready.

Try it yourself: A sheet has the columns 'Q1 sales', 'Q2 sales', 'Q3 sales', 'Q4 sales'. How would you make it tidy?

Model answer. Make one column called Quarter and one called Sales, so each product has four rows (one per quarter). In Power Query this is Unpivot Columns.

Check what you just learned

1. Which layout is tidy?
  • A column for each month
  • Totals typed between groups
  • Merged heading cells
  • One row per product and month with a Sales column (correct)

Month is a column, so you can filter and group by it.

2. Why keep the raw data untouched?
  • You can redo or correct the cleaning later (correct)
  • It takes less space
  • Excel requires it
  • It is faster

A correction is only possible if the original survives.
keyPoints: Tidy data: one variable per column, one observation per row, one kind of thing per table.
Months or categories in column headings, merged cells, blank rows and typed-in totals are the common problems.
Never overwrite the raw data; clean a copy.

topics.title: Cleaning text and numbers with formulas
topics.html:
Text from exports and forms arrives in uneven shape. A small set of functions fixes most of it.

The cleaning toolkit
ProblemFunctionExample → result
Extra spacesTRIMTRIM(" asha rao ") → asha rao
Inconsistent capitalsPROPER, UPPER, LOWERPROPER("BILAL khan") → Bilal Khan
Unwanted charactersSUBSTITUTESUBSTITUTE("Rs 1200", "Rs ", "") → 1200
Text that should be a numberVALUEVALUE("1200") → 1200
Pieces of textLEFT, RIGHT, MID, LENLEFT("PUNE-411001", 4) → PUNE
Find a characterFIND, SEARCHFIND("-", "PUNE-411001") → 5
Join pieces&, TEXTJOINA2 & " " & B2

Functions can be nested: the inner one runs first. =PROPER(TRIM(A2)) first removes extra spaces and then fixes the capitals. To turn Rs 1200 into a number you remove the text and convert what is left: =VALUE(SUBSTITUTE(C2, "Rs ", "")).

Formula · A cleaning formula, built inside-out

=VALUE(SUBSTITUTE(C2, "Rs ", ""))

SUBSTITUTE removes the prefix, VALUE turns the remaining text into a real number you can add up.

Worked example

Splitting a code

A product code looks like PUNE-411001. Get the city part and the pin code separately.

  1. Find the dash: FIND("-", A2) gives 5.
  2. City = the characters before it: LEFT(A2, FIND("-", A2) - 1) → PUNE.
  3. Pin = everything after it: MID(A2, FIND("-", A2) + 1, 10) → 411001.

Answer. Combining FIND with LEFT and MID splits any code with a separator.

Watch out

A number stored as text is the most common hidden error. It looks right but SUM ignores it, so totals come out too small. Left-aligned numbers, a small green triangle, or ISNUMBER(A2) returning FALSE are the signs.

Tip

Do cleaning in helper columns beside the raw column, then copy and Paste Special → Values over the result when you are happy. The raw column stays as your evidence.

Common mistakes

  • Typing the cleaned values by hand. Use formulas so the step can be repeated on new data.
  • Forgetting that TRIM does not remove non-breaking spaces copied from web pages; use SUBSTITUTE(A2, CHAR(160), " ") first.
  • Using VALUE on text that still contains a currency symbol or comma. Remove those first.

Check what you just learned

1. Which formula turns "Rs 850" into the number 850?
  • =TRIM(A1)
  • =VALUE(SUBSTITUTE(A1,"Rs ","")) (correct)
  • =PROPER(A1)
  • =LEFT(A1,2)

Remove the prefix with SUBSTITUTE and convert with VALUE.

2. `=PROPER(TRIM(A2))` first:
  • Capitalises, then trims
  • Counts characters
  • Trims, then capitalises (correct)
  • Deletes the cell

The inner function, TRIM, runs first.
keyPoints: TRIM, PROPER and SUBSTITUTE clean text; VALUE turns text into a number.
Nest functions: the inner one runs first.
A number stored as text is ignored by SUM: test with ISNUMBER.

topics.title: Dates, duplicates and checking quality
topics.html:
Dates are numbers underneath: Excel stores a date as a count of days, so subtracting two dates gives the days between them and TEXT can show any part of one. In this course's sheet, a date typed as 2025-03-09 (year-month-day) is understood everywhere.

Date tools
You wantUseResult for 2025-03-09
The month as textTEXT(A2, "mmm")Mar
The weekdayTEXT(A2, "dddd")Sunday
Year, month, day numbersYEAR, MONTH, DAY2025, 3, 9
Days between datesB2 - A2 or DAYS(B2, A2)a number of days
Build a dateDATE(2025, 4, 1)1 April 2025
Last day of the monthEOMONTH(A2, 0)31 March 2025

Duplicates need a decision. Two identical rows might be the same order entered twice, or two genuine orders for the same item. Mark them first, then decide: =COUNTIF($A$2:A2, A2) > 1 is TRUE from the second appearance of a value downward, so it flags the repeats without deleting anything.

Finally, check quality before you analyse. Four quick questions catch most trouble:

A data quality checklist

  • Complete: how many blanks in each column? (COUNTBLANK)
  • Valid: are values in a sensible range? (MIN, MAX: a negative age or a 2099 date is a clue)
  • Unique: are keys repeated when they should not be? (COUNTIF)
  • Consistent: is each thing spelled one way? (sort or filter the column and look)
Worked example

A five-minute audit

A sales sheet has 2,000 rows and a Units column.

  1. =COUNTBLANK(D2:D2001) returns 14: fourteen blanks to explain.
  2. =MIN(D2:D2001) returns -3 and =MAX(D2:D2001) returns 4000: a negative and a suspicious high.
  3. Look at those rows. The -3 is a return; the 4000 is a typo for 40.

Answer. Three formulas found three problems before a single chart was drawn.

What bad data does to a total

A column has numbers stored as text, which SUM ignores. See how big the error becomes.

Adjust Rows in the column, Rows stored as text (%), Average value per row and see True total, What SUM shows, Missing from the total change.

Common mistakes

  • Deleting duplicates before deciding whether they are real.
  • Treating a blank as zero. A missing value and a value of zero are different facts.
  • Skipping the quality check because the data came from a trusted system.
Try it yourself: Write a formula that returns TRUE when a value in A5 has already appeared above it in A2:A5.

Model answer. =COUNTIF($A$2:A4, A5) > 0 (or COUNTIF($A$2:A5, A5) > 1).

Check what you just learned

1. How do you get the weekday name of a date in A2?
  • =DAY(A2)
  • =LEN(A2)
  • =A2+7
  • =TEXT(A2,"dddd") (correct)

TEXT with "dddd" gives the full day name.

2. Which formula counts blanks in D2:D100?
  • =COUNTBLANK(D2:D100) (correct)
  • =COUNTA(D2:D100)
  • =COUNT(D2:D100)
  • =SUM(D2:D100)

COUNTBLANK counts empty cells.
keyPoints: Dates are numbers: subtract to get days; use TEXT, YEAR, MONTH and DATE to take them apart or build them.
Flag duplicates with COUNTIF before deciding what to remove.
Audit completeness, validity, uniqueness and consistency before analysing.

topics.title: Power Query thinking: record the steps
topics.html:
Power Query is the data-preparation tool built into Excel (Data tab → Get Data). Instead of editing cells, you build a list of applied steps: remove blank rows, trim text, change a type, unpivot columns. Each step is recorded, so when next month's export arrives you press Refresh and every step runs again. Power Query runs in desktop Excel and Power BI, not in this browser, so here you practise the same thinking with formulas.

The same step, two ways
Cleaning stepWith formulas (this course's sheet)In Power Query (desktop Excel)
Remove extra spacesTRIMTransform → Format → Trim
Fix capitalsPROPERTransform → Format → Capitalize Each Word
Text to numberVALUE(SUBSTITUTE(...))Replace Values, then change the column type
Split a codeLEFT / MID / FINDSplit Column → By Delimiter
Months in columns to rowsRebuild the table by handTransform → Unpivot Columns
Remove blank rowsFilter and deleteHome → Remove Rows → Remove Blank Rows
Worked example

What 'refreshable' buys you

Every month the finance team sends a CSV with 6,000 rows and the same problems.

  1. Build the cleaning once as applied steps, saved with the workbook.
  2. Next month, replace the CSV and press Data → Refresh All.
  3. The same eight steps run in seconds, with no manual clicking.

Answer. A repeatable process saves hours and removes the mistakes people make when they redo manual cleaning.

Watch out

Power Query is not available in the browser version of this course. The labs here teach the formulas and the thinking. If you have desktop Excel, repeat the exercises there with Get Data to see the same steps recorded.

Habits that make any cleaning repeatable

  • Write down each step in order, even if you do it by formula.
  • Never fix a value by typing over it; change the rule instead.
  • Keep raw data, cleaned data and results on separate sheets.
  • Name your steps and tables so someone else can follow them.

Common mistakes

  • Cleaning by hand and forgetting what you did.
  • Changing the source file's layout, which breaks the saved steps.
  • Loading cleaned data on top of the raw sheet.

Check what you just learned

1. The main benefit of Power Query's applied steps is that they:
  • Make the file smaller
  • Can be re-run on new data with one Refresh (correct)
  • Remove the need for a source
  • Change the raw file

A recorded pipeline is repeatable.

2. Which Power Query command turns month columns into rows?
  • Pivot Column
  • Merge Queries
  • Unpivot Columns (correct)
  • Group By

Unpivot makes the data tidy.

Key terms: flip and sort

Tidy data
One variable per column, one observation per row.
Unpivot
Turn column headings (such as months) into values in a column.
TRIM
Removes extra spaces from text.
VALUE
Converts text that looks like a number into a real number.
Applied steps
The recorded list of cleaning steps in Power Query.
Helper column
A column of formulas beside the raw data.
Data quality
Complete, valid, unique and consistent.
keyPoints: Power Query records cleaning as repeatable steps that Refresh re-runs.
Every cleaning step has a formula equivalent; do it in helper columns and write the steps down.
Keep raw, cleaned and result data apart.

modules.title: Describe the data: centre, spread and outliers
modules.summary: Summarise a column with the right statistics, find unusual values, and show the shape of the data with a histogram.
modules.outcome: You can choose between mean, median and mode, measure spread with standard deviation and quartiles, flag outliers with the IQR rule, standardise values with z-scores and build a histogram with COUNTIFS.
modules.intro: Before modelling or forecasting, describe what you have. A good description answers four questions: What is typical? How much does it vary? Is anything unusual? What shape is the distribution? Excel has a function for each, and knowing which to trust is half the skill. This module uses a small daily-sales table with one suspicious value, so you see in numbers why the average alone can mislead.

topics.title: Centre: mean, median and mode
topics.html:
Three statistics describe what is 'typical', and they answer slightly different questions.

Measures of centre
MeasureExcelWhat it isBest used when
Mean (average)AVERAGETotal divided by the countData is roughly symmetric, with no extreme values
MedianMEDIANThe middle value when sortedData is skewed or has outliers (incomes, house prices, delivery times)
ModeMODEThe most frequent valueCategories or repeated whole numbers (the most common shoe size)
Worked example

One value changes the story

Daily sales (units) for 12 days: 18, 22, 20, 19, 23, 21, 20, 24, 22, 19, 21, and 96 (a bulk order).

  1. Mean = 325 / 12, about 27.1 units.
  2. Median: sort the data; the middle two values are 21 and 21, so the median is 21.
  3. Eleven of the twelve days are between 18 and 24, yet the mean says 27. The mean has been pulled up by one day.

Answer. The median (21) describes a typical day; the mean (27.1) describes the total spread over days, including the bulk order. Report both and explain the gap.

Change the twelfth day and watch the mean move

Eleven ordinary days total 229 units. Change the twelfth day and see what happens to the mean.

Adjust The twelfth day (units) and see Mean of all 12 days, Mean of the 11 ordinary days, Median of all 12 days (while the twelfth day is above 21) change.

Watch out

Whenever mean and median are far apart, the data is skewed or has an outlier. Do not choose the more flattering number: say why they differ.

Common mistakes

  • Quoting only the mean. It hides skew.
  • Using AVERAGE on a column that includes zeros that really mean 'not recorded'.
  • Reporting a mode when every value is different. MODE then returns an error, which is the honest answer.
Try it yourself: Five salaries: 30,000, 32,000, 33,000, 35,000 and 400,000. Which is the better 'typical salary': mean or median?

Model answer. The median, 33,000. The mean (106,000) is dragged up by the one very large salary.

Check what you just learned

1. Which measure is least affected by one extreme value?
  • Mean
  • Maximum
  • Sum
  • Median (correct)

The middle value does not move when the largest value grows.

2. `=MODE(A1:A8)` where every value is different returns:
  • An error (#N/A) (correct)
  • The first value
  • 0
  • The average

There is no most frequent value.
keyPoints: Mean is sensitive to extreme values; median is robust; mode is the most frequent value.
If the mean and median differ a lot, look for skew or outliers.
Report more than one measure and explain gaps.

topics.title: Spread: range, standard deviation and quartiles
topics.html:
Two columns can have the same average and very different behaviour: one steady, one wild. Spread measures that.

Measures of spread
MeasureExcelMeaning
RangeMAX - MINDistance from lowest to highest; very sensitive to outliers
Standard deviation (sample)STDEV.STypical distance from the mean; use for a sample of a larger group
Standard deviation (population)STDEV.PUse when your data is the whole group
VarianceVAR.S, VAR.PThe square of the standard deviation
QuartilesQUARTILE(range, 1) and QUARTILE(range, 3)The values below which 25% and 75% of the data fall
Interquartile range (IQR)Q3 - Q1The spread of the middle half; robust to outliers
PercentilePERCENTILE(range, 0.9)The value below which 90% of the data falls
Formula · Sample standard deviation

s = √( Σ(x − mean)² ÷ (n − 1) )

Divide by n − 1 for a sample (STDEV.S) and by n for the whole population (STDEV.P).

Worked example

Reading a standard deviation

Delivery times average 30 minutes with a standard deviation of 4 minutes.

  1. Roughly two thirds of deliveries fall within one standard deviation: 26 to 34 minutes.
  2. About 95% fall within two: 22 to 38 minutes.
  3. A delivery taking 50 minutes is 5 standard deviations out, so it is very unusual.

Answer. The standard deviation turns 'how different is this value?' into a number you can compare. (The two-thirds and 95% figures hold for roughly bell-shaped data.)

Same average, different steadiness

Two teams average the same. See how the standard deviation changes what you expect on a given day.

Adjust Average (minutes), Standard deviation (minutes) and see Most days are between (low), Most days are between (high), Nearly all days (2 sd, low), Nearly all days (2 sd, high) change.

Watch out

STDEV.S and STDEV.P give different answers. For a sample (survey respondents, last 30 days from a longer history), use .S. If the data is the entire population, use .P. When unsure, .S is the safe default for analysis.

Common mistakes

  • Reporting an average without any measure of spread.
  • Mixing up STDEV.S and STDEV.P.
  • Using the range for skewed data: one outlier sets it.
Try it yourself: Write the formula for the interquartile range of data in A2:A50.

Model answer. =QUARTILE(A2:A50,3)-QUARTILE(A2:A50,1)

Check what you just learned

1. Which statistic describes the spread of the middle 50% of the data?
  • Mean
  • Interquartile range (correct)
  • Range
  • Mode

IQR = Q3 − Q1.

2. For data that is a sample of a larger group you use:
  • STDEV.P
  • AVERAGE
  • STDEV.S (correct)
  • MEDIAN

A sample uses n − 1 in the denominator.
keyPoints: Standard deviation measures typical distance from the mean; quartiles and IQR describe the middle half.
Use STDEV.S for a sample and STDEV.P for a whole population.
Always report spread beside the average.

topics.title: Outliers and z-scores
topics.html:
An outlier is a value far from the others. It might be an error (a typo, a unit mistake), a genuine rare event (a bulk order), or a sign something changed. Spotting it is a calculation; deciding what it is, is a judgement.

Two standard rules

  • The IQR rule: a value is an outlier if it is above Q3 + 1.5 × IQR or below Q1 − 1.5 × IQR. It does not assume a bell shape, and the outlier itself does not distort the quartiles much.
  • The z-score rule: a value more than 2 or 3 standard deviations from the mean is unusual. It is easy to compare across columns, but an extreme outlier inflates the standard deviation and can hide itself.
Formula · z-score

z = (x − mean) ÷ standard deviation

In Excel: =STANDARDIZE(x, mean, stdev). A z-score says how many standard deviations a value is from the mean.

Worked example

The IQR rule on the sales data

Daily sales: 18, 19, 19, 20, 20, 21, 21, 22, 22, 23, 24, 96.

  1. Q1 = QUARTILE(range,1) = 19.75 and Q3 = QUARTILE(range,3) = 22.25.
  2. IQR = 22.25 − 19.75 = 2.5, so the upper fence is 22.25 + 1.5 × 2.5 = 26.
  3. Only 96 is above 26: one outlier, as expected.

Answer. Counting values above the fence with COUNTIF(range, ">"&fence) gives 1.

Worked example

Comparing two exams with z-scores

Anil scored 78 on a test with mean 70 and standard deviation 8. Beena scored 85 on a test with mean 80 and standard deviation 10.

  1. Anil: z = (78 − 70) / 8 = 1.0.
  2. Beena: z = (85 − 80) / 10 = 0.5.
  3. NORM.S.DIST(z, TRUE) converts z to a percentile for bell-shaped data: 0.84 for Anil and 0.69 for Beena.

Answer. Anil did better relative to his class even though Beena's raw mark is higher.

Watch out

Never delete an outlier just because it is an outlier. Ask what caused it. A typo can be corrected, a rare real event might be the most important thing in the data. If you exclude it, say so and show the result with and without it.

Common mistakes

  • Removing outliers to make a chart look neater.
  • Using the z-score rule on very small samples, where one value dominates the mean and SD.
  • Applying a bell-curve conversion (NORM.S.DIST) to data that is not roughly bell shaped.
Try it yourself: A value has z = −2.5. What does that mean?

Model answer. It is 2.5 standard deviations below the mean: unusually low, rare in bell-shaped data.

Check what you just learned

1. A z-score of 0 means the value is:
  • The maximum
  • Negative
  • An outlier
  • Equal to the mean (correct)

It is zero standard deviations from the mean.

2. What should you do with a flagged outlier?
  • Investigate its cause, then decide and document (correct)
  • Delete it
  • Ignore the chart
  • Double it

Judgement, not automation.
keyPoints: The IQR rule flags values beyond Q1 − 1.5×IQR or Q3 + 1.5×IQR; z-scores count standard deviations from the mean.
STANDARDIZE and NORM.S.DIST compare values across different scales.
Investigate outliers; do not delete them automatically.

topics.title: Shape: histograms with COUNTIFS
topics.html:
A histogram counts how many values fall into each range ('bin'), showing the shape of the data: a single hump, two humps, a long tail. It answers questions a single average cannot: are most orders small with a few huge ones? Is there a second group of customers?

The ">="&E2 pattern joins an operator and a cell value into a condition. Use >= lower and < upper, so a value that sits exactly on a boundary lands in one bin only. The counts should add up to the number of values: if they do not, a bin boundary is wrong.

A histogram table
Bin labelLowerUpperCount
0 to 990100…
100 to 199100200…
200 to 299200300…
300 and above300100000…
Tip

Choose the number of bins to suit the data: too few hides the shape, too many makes noise. Five to ten bins is a good start for a few hundred values.

Common mistakes

  • Bins that overlap or leave gaps, so values are counted twice or not at all.
  • Uneven bin widths without saying so, which distorts the picture.
  • Forgetting to check that the counts add up to the total.
Try it yourself: What goes in the Count cell for the bin 100 to 199 if the bounds are in E3 and F3?

Model answer. =COUNTIFS($A$2:$A$41,">="&E3,$A$2:$A$41,"<"&F3)

Check what you just learned

1. Why use >= lower and < upper for bins?
  • It is shorter
  • So each value falls in exactly one bin (correct)
  • Excel requires it
  • It ignores blanks

A value on the boundary belongs to one bin only.

2. A histogram shows:
  • Trends over time
  • Totals by category
  • How values are distributed across ranges (correct)
  • Correlation

It shows the shape of the distribution.

Key terms: flip and sort

Mean
Total divided by the count.
Median
The middle value when sorted.
Standard deviation
Typical distance from the mean.
Quartile
A value below which 25%, 50% or 75% of the data falls.
IQR
Q3 minus Q1: the spread of the middle half.
Outlier
A value far from the others.
z-score
How many standard deviations a value is from the mean.
Histogram
A count of values per bin.
keyPoints: A histogram counts values per bin to show the distribution's shape.
Use >= lower and < upper so every value falls in exactly one bin.
Check that bin counts add up to the total.

modules.title: Summarise like a pivot table
modules.summary: Break totals down by category with SUMIFS and COUNTIFS, build a cross-tab, find the vital few with a Pareto analysis, and avoid the ratio traps.
modules.outcome: You can build a cross-tab with mixed references, rank items and compute cumulative shares, classify products A/B/C, and calculate rates correctly as a ratio of sums.
modules.intro: Raw rows do not answer questions; summaries do. Which region sells most? Which five products make up most of the revenue? What is the real conversion rate across all channels? A pivot table answers these in two clicks, but the formulas behind it (SUMIFS, COUNTIFS and a little arithmetic) give you control, transparency and the ability to explain every number. This module teaches the formulas, and shows where the same ideas live in a PivotTable on the desktop.

topics.title: SUMIFS, COUNTIFS and the cross-tab
topics.html:
A cross-tab (the heart of a pivot table) shows one measure broken down by two categories, with one category down the side and one across the top. The cell at each crossing is a conditional total: SUMIFS(values, category-1 range, category-1 value, category-2 range, category-2 value).

The data
RegionProductUnitsRevenue
NorthPen10100
SouthPen20200
NorthBook5250
EastPen770
…………
The cross-tab you want
RevenuePenBookTotal
North………
South………
East………
Total………

One formula, written once with mixed references, fills the entire grid. The region comes from column F and the product from row 1 of the grid, so lock them with dollar signs:

Formula · One formula for the whole grid

=SUMIFS($D$2:$D$11, $A$2:$A$11, $F2, $B$2:$B$11, G$1)

$F2 keeps the column fixed so the region always comes from column F; G$1 keeps the row fixed so the product always comes from the header row; the $D$2:$D$11 ranges are fully locked.

Worked example

Reading the formula

In cell G2 the formula above is copied right to H2 and down to G3.

  1. Copied right: G$1 becomes H$1, so it picks up Book instead of Pen.
  2. Copied down: $F2 becomes $F3, so it picks up South instead of North.
  3. The locked ranges never move.

Answer. Mixed references are what make a single formula correct in every cell.

How the cross-tab total is built

Change units and price for Pen and Book in the North, and see the cell and row totals.

Adjust North Pen revenue, North Book revenue, All other regions' revenue and see North row total, Grand total, North's share change.

Tip

Always add a Total row and column, and check that the grand total equals SUM of the original column. If it does not, a category is missing or misspelled.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting the dollar signs, so the ranges slide down as you copy and the totals are wrong.
  • A trailing space in a category (North ) means SUMIFS finds nothing for it: clean first.
  • Criteria that are mixed up between the two categories, so values land in the wrong cells.
Try it yourself: What does =COUNTIFS($A$2:$A$11,$F2,$B$2:$B$11,G$1) return?

Model answer. The number of rows where the region equals the row label and the product equals the column heading: the count of sales for that crossing.

Check what you just learned

1. In `$F2`, the dollar sign:
  • Locks the row
  • Does nothing
  • Formats currency
  • Locks the column (correct)

$ before the column letter fixes the column.

2. Which function counts rows that meet two conditions?
  • COUNTIFS (correct)
  • COUNTIF
  • SUMIF
  • COUNTA

COUNTIFS takes pairs of range and condition.
keyPoints: A cross-tab is a conditional total per pair of categories: SUMIFS with two criteria.
Mixed references ($F2 and G$1) let one formula fill the whole grid.
Check the grand total against the original column.

topics.title: Pareto analysis: finding the vital few
topics.html:
In many businesses a small share of items produces most of the result: a few products make most of the revenue, a few customers cause most of the complaints. The Pareto principle (often called the 80/20 rule) is a useful pattern, not a law, and a Pareto analysis measures it for your data.

Items sorted by revenue
ProductRevenueShareCumulativeClass
Laptop52040.0%40.0%A
Phone31023.8%63.8%A
Tablet19014.6%78.5%A
Watch1209.2%87.7%B
Earbuds906.9%94.6%B
Cable403.1%97.7%C
Case302.3%100.0%C

The share is the item's revenue divided by the total (=B2/$B$9). The cumulative share adds it to the share above (=D2+C3). Class uses thresholds: A while the cumulative share is up to 80%, B up to 95%, C for the rest. =IF(D2<=0.8,"A",IF(D2<=0.95,"B","C")).

Worked example

What the table tells a manager

Three of seven products (43% of the range) bring in 78% of the revenue.

  1. Class A items deserve protection: never out of stock, best shelf space.
  2. Class C items add little (5%) but cost shelf space, stock and attention.
  3. Before deleting them, check why: a cable may be the item that makes laptop buyers return.

Answer. Pareto tells you where to look first. It does not tell you what to do: that takes judgement about the business.

Watch out

The sort matters. The cumulative share is only meaningful when items are sorted from largest to smallest. If you sort after building the formulas, re-check them.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting to lock the total ($B$9) so it slides as you copy the formula down.
  • Treating '80/20' as exact. The real split may be 70/30 or 90/10.
  • Classifying by count of items instead of by cumulative value.
Try it yourself: What is the cumulative share of the first two products in the table?

Model answer. 63.8%: 40.0% + 23.8% (830 out of 1,300).

Check what you just learned

1. The cumulative share of the first row equals:
  • 0
  • Its own share (correct)
  • 100%
  • The total

The first row has nothing above it to add.

2. For Pareto analysis items must be sorted:
  • Alphabetically
  • Randomly
  • Largest to smallest (correct)
  • By date

Cumulative share only makes sense in descending order.
keyPoints: Pareto analysis sorts items by value and tracks the cumulative share.
A/B/C classes focus attention: A is the vital few.
Lock the total so each row's share divides by the same number.

topics.title: Rates, ratios and averages done right
topics.html:
Many headline numbers are ratios: conversion rate, average order value, defect rate. A frequent mistake is to average the ratios instead of dividing the totals. They are not the same.

Conversion by channel
ChannelVisitsOrdersRate
Email1,000505%
Ads2002010%
Social501020%
Worked example

Two ways to get 'the overall rate'

Which is the real conversion rate across all channels?

  1. Average of the three rates: (5% + 10% + 20%) / 3 = 11.7%.
  2. Ratio of the totals: total orders / total visits = 80 / 1,250 = 6.4%.
  3. Email brings most of the visitors, and those convert at 5%. The overall rate must be near 5%, not 11.7%.

Answer. The correct overall rate is 6.4%: the sum of orders divided by the sum of visits. Averaging the rates gives every channel equal weight, which they do not deserve.

Formula · Weighted correctness

overall rate = SUM(part) ÷ SUM(whole)

Always add the numerators and the denominators first, then divide once.

Other ratio traps

  • Average of averages: the average of each region's average order value is not the company's average order value; divide total revenue by total orders.
  • Percent of percent: a rise from 5% to 6% is one percentage point, and a 20% relative increase. Say which.
  • Small denominators: 3 of 4 is 75%, but it is little evidence. Show the count beside the rate.
  • Dividing by zero: wrap risky divisions with IFERROR or IF, and show a dash rather than a misleading 0.
Watch out

This trap is so common it has a name: Simpson's paradox is when a trend that appears in every group reverses when the groups are combined, usually because the groups have different sizes. Whenever you combine groups, compare the weights.

Common mistakes

  • Calling AVERAGE on a column of percentages.
  • Hiding the denominator.
  • Reporting a rate with no time period.
Try it yourself: Region A has 10 orders worth 1,000 in total; region B has 90 orders worth 18,000. What is the overall average order value?

Model answer. (1,000 + 18,000) / (10 + 90) = 190. The average of 100 and 200 is 150, which is wrong.

Check what you just learned

1. The correct overall conversion rate is:
  • The average of each channel's rate
  • The median rate
  • The highest rate
  • Total orders divided by total visits (correct)

Divide the sums.

2. A rise from 5% to 6% is:
  • One percentage point (correct)
  • 1%
  • Impossible
  • 6 points

State percentage points or relative change.
keyPoints: Overall rate = total part ÷ total whole, not the average of rates.
An average of averages ignores group sizes.
Show counts beside percentages and guard against dividing by zero.

topics.title: Pivot tables and Power Pivot: what they do for you
topics.html:
Everything in this module can be done with a PivotTable on the desktop: select a tidy table, choose Insert → PivotTable, and drag fields into Rows, Columns and Values. The formulas you learned explain what the pivot does, so you can check it and recreate it when needed.

Pivot concepts and their formulas
In a PivotTableThe formula equivalent
Rows and Columns fieldsThe category labels down the side and across the top
Values: Sum of RevenueSUMIFS with the row and column categories as conditions
Values: Count of OrderCOUNTIFS
Show values as % of Grand TotalCell ÷ the grand total cell
Filters and SlicersA criterion in the SUMIFS, or a filter on the data
Grouping dates by monthA helper column with TEXT(date, "yyyy-mm")

Power Pivot and the Data Model go further: they let a PivotTable use several related tables (sales, customers, products) without lookups, and DAX measures such as Total Revenue := SUM(Sales[Revenue]) that are calculated in the context of each pivot cell. This works in desktop Excel (some editions) and in Power BI, and is the subject of the Power BI course in this category. It does not run in the browser here.

When to choose a pivot, and when a formula

  • Pivot for exploring: quick, flexible, easy to change.
  • Formulas for fixed reports, dashboards and checks: transparent and stable.
  • Power Pivot or Power BI when you have several tables or millions of rows.
Watch out

A PivotTable does not update on its own when the source changes: use Data → Refresh All. A very common source of out-of-date reports.

Tip

If a pivot total looks wrong, rebuild one cell with SUMIFS. If the two agree, the pivot is right and the question was different; if not, check for blanks, text numbers or filtered items.

Common mistakes

  • Pivoting a range with blank rows or a total row.
  • Forgetting to refresh.
  • Trusting a pivot without a sanity check against the source total.

Check what you just learned

1. A PivotTable 'Sum of Revenue' is equivalent to:
  • COUNTA
  • SUMIFS (correct)
  • VLOOKUP
  • TEXT

It is a conditional total by the row and column categories.

2. A pivot is out of date after the source changes until you:
  • Save
  • Sort
  • Refresh (correct)
  • Close

Use Refresh All.

Key terms: flip and sort

Cross-tab
A table of a measure by two categories.
SUMIFS
Adds values that meet several conditions.
Mixed reference
A reference with one part locked, like $F2 or G
Pareto analysis
Ranking items by value to find the vital few.
Cumulative share
The running total of shares from the largest item down.
PivotTable
An Excel tool that builds cross-tabs by drag and drop.
Simpson's paradox
A trend that reverses when groups are combined.
keyPoints: A PivotTable is a conditional total per category: the same maths as SUMIFS.
Power Pivot and DAX extend this to related tables; they run in desktop tools.
Always reconcile a pivot to the source total.

modules.title: Relationships, regression and trends
modules.summary: Measure how two things move together, fit a straight line to forecast, and separate trend from seasonality in time series.
modules.outcome: You can calculate and interpret correlation and R², fit a line with SLOPE and INTERCEPT, forecast with FORECAST, smooth a series with a moving average and compute seasonal indexes, and say honestly how much to trust each.
modules.intro: Does more advertising lead to more sales? Do hot days raise ice-cream sales? Will next quarter be higher than this one? These questions need a relationship or a trend, and Excel can measure both. This module also teaches the discipline that protects you from embarrassing claims: a correlation is not a cause, a forecast is a range not a number, and a line fitted to six points tells you much less than it appears to.

topics.title: Correlation: do two things move together?
topics.html:
The correlation coefficient (r) measures how closely two numeric columns move together, on a scale from −1 to +1. Plot the points first: a scatter chart shows the relationship, and the number summarises it.

Reading r
rWhat it means
+1A perfect upward straight line
+0.7A strong positive relationship: when x is high, y tends to be high
0No straight-line relationship
−0.7A strong negative relationship: when x is high, y tends to be low
−1A perfect downward straight line
Formula · Correlation in Excel

=CORREL(y_range, x_range)

Order does not matter for CORREL. Both ranges must be the same size, numbers only.

Squaring r gives R², the share of the variation in y that a straight line on x accounts for. With r = 0.77, R² = 0.60: the line explains about 60% of the ups and downs, and 40% is left unexplained.

From r to R²

Move r and see how much of the variation a straight line explains.

Adjust Correlation r (as a number from 0 to 1) and see R squared, Share of variation explained, Share left unexplained change.

Watch out

Correlation is not causation. Ice-cream sales and drownings both rise in summer: the hidden cause is hot weather (a confounder). Before you claim 'A causes B', ask: could B cause A? Could a third thing drive both? Could it be chance, especially with few points?

Worked example

Reading a result honestly

Weekly ad spend and sales for 8 weeks give r = 0.85.

  1. Strong positive relationship: weeks with more ads had higher sales.
  2. R² = 0.72: ad spend accounts for about 72% of the variation in these 8 weeks.
  3. But all 8 weeks are in the festive season. The ads and the sales may both be driven by the season.

Answer. Say: 'In these weeks, higher ad spend went with higher sales. We have not shown it caused them.' A controlled test would.

Common mistakes

  • Quoting r without drawing the scatter. Curves, clusters and outliers can give a misleading r.
  • Treating r = 0.3 as 'strong'. Check the scatter and the sample size.
  • Claiming causation from correlation.
Try it yourself: If r = −0.9 between price and units sold, what does it say?

Model answer. Strongly negative: in this data higher prices went with lower sales. It does not prove price caused the drop.

Check what you just learned

1. r = 0 means:
  • No relationship of any kind
  • Negative
  • A perfect fit
  • No straight-line relationship (correct)

There could still be a curved relationship.

2. Two things rise together in summer. The most likely explanation is:
  • A confounder such as the weather (correct)
  • One causes the other
  • Bad data
  • A formula error

A third factor drives both.
keyPoints: CORREL measures straight-line association from −1 to +1; R² is r squared.
Always chart the data; r alone can mislead.
Correlation does not show causation: look for confounders.

topics.title: Regression: fit a line and forecast
topics.html:
Linear regression finds the straight line that best fits the points: y = intercept + slope × x. The slope says how much y changes for one unit more of x. The intercept is the predicted y when x is 0, which may or may not mean anything real.

The regression functions
FunctionReturns
SLOPE(known_y, known_x)Change in y per unit of x
INTERCEPT(known_y, known_x)Predicted y when x = 0
RSQ(known_y, known_x)R²: the share of variation explained
FORECAST(x, known_y, known_x)The predicted y for a new x
Worked example

Five points

x (ad spend, ₹ thousand): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. y (sales, ₹ lakh): 2, 4, 5, 4, 5.

  1. =SLOPE(B2:B6, A2:A6) = 0.6: each extra ₹1,000 of ads goes with ₹0.6 lakh more sales.
  2. =INTERCEPT(B2:B6, A2:A6) = 2.2.
  3. =RSQ(B2:B6, A2:A6) = 0.6: the line explains 60% of the variation.
  4. =FORECAST(6, B2:B6, A2:A6) = 2.2 + 0.6 × 6 = 5.8.

Answer. At ₹6 thousand of ads, the line predicts ₹5.8 lakh of sales, if the pattern continues.

Predict with a line

The line from the example: intercept 2.2 and slope 0.6. Choose a spend and see the prediction.

Adjust Ad spend (₹ thousand) and see Predicted sales (₹ lakh), Distance beyond the fitted range of 1 to 5 change.

Watch out

Extrapolation is risky. The line was fitted on spends between 1 and 5. A prediction at 6 is a small step; at 50 it is a guess, because the real relationship may flatten (diminishing returns) or break. Stay close to the range of your data, and say when you leave it.

Questions to ask of any regression

  • How many points? Six points are a sketch, not a model.
  • Is the scatter roughly a straight line? If it curves, a line misleads.
  • Is R² reasonable for the field? 0.3 may be useful in social data and poor in physics.
  • Are there outliers pulling the line?
  • Is the prediction inside the range of the data?

Common mistakes

  • Swapping known_y and known_x: the order is (y, x).
  • Predicting far outside the range of x.
  • Reporting a forecast as a single exact number.
Try it yourself: Using slope 0.6 and intercept 2.2, what sales does the line predict at x = 3?

Model answer. 2.2 + 0.6 × 3 = 4.0.

Check what you just learned

1. The slope of a regression line is:
  • The value of y when x is 0
  • The change in y for one more unit of x (correct)
  • R squared
  • The average of x

It is the rate of change.

2. Why is predicting far outside your data risky?
  • Excel refuses
  • It is slow
  • The relationship may change outside the range (correct)
  • The slope turns negative

You have no evidence about the pattern there.
keyPoints: y = intercept + slope × x; SLOPE, INTERCEPT, RSQ and FORECAST give the pieces.
R² says how much of the variation the line explains.
Do not extrapolate far beyond the data; state uncertainty.

topics.title: Time series: trend, moving average and seasonality
topics.html:
Business data over time mixes three things: a trend (the long-run direction), seasonality (a repeating pattern, such as festive-season peaks) and noise (random variation). To see the trend, smooth the noise.

Formula · Moving average

MA(3) in month t = (sales t−2 + sales t−1 + sales t) ÷ 3

In Excel: =AVERAGE(B2:B4) in row 4, copied down. Each value averages the latest three months.

A three-month moving average
MonthSales3-month average
1100
2120
3110110
4130120
5150130

The moving average starts in month 3 (the first month with three values), and it lags a little behind the data, which is the price of smoothness. A longer window smooths more and lags more.

Seasonality is measured with a seasonal index: each period's value divided by the average of all periods. An index of 1.2 means that period is 20% above normal; 0.8 means 20% below.

Worked example

Quarterly seasonal index

Quarterly sales: 80, 120, 100, 100.

  1. Average = 400 / 4 = 100.
  2. Index = value ÷ average: 0.8, 1.2, 1.0, 1.0.
  3. Quarter 2 is typically 20% above an average quarter; Quarter 1 is 20% below.

Answer. To compare quarters fairly or to plan stock, multiply a forecast of 'an average quarter' by each quarter's index.

Seasonality in action

Plan next year's quarter using the seasonal index.

Adjust Expected average quarter (units), This quarter's seasonal index and see Expected sales this quarter, Difference from an average quarter change.

Watch out

Compare like with like. December against November includes the festive effect. For growth, compare with the same month last year, or use the seasonal index first. A moving average of 12 months removes seasonality entirely.

Common mistakes

  • Calling a seasonal peak 'growth'.
  • Using a moving average of 3 months on data with a yearly pattern.
  • Forgetting that the first few periods have no moving average.
Try it yourself: An index of 0.75 for January means:

Model answer. January is typically 25% below an average month.

Check what you just learned

1. A seasonal index of 1.2 means the period is:
  • 20% below average
  • 120 units
  • Equal to average
  • 20% above average (correct)

1.2 times normal.

2. A longer moving-average window:
  • Smooths more and lags more (correct)
  • Smooths less
  • Has no effect
  • Removes zeros

More points averaged means a smoother, slower line.
keyPoints: Time series combine trend, seasonality and noise.
A moving average smooths noise; a seasonal index shows the repeating pattern.
Compare the same period last year, or adjust for seasonality, before claiming growth.

topics.title: Forecasting honestly
topics.html:
A forecast is a statement about the future based on the past, and it is always uncertain. A good analyst gives a number, a range, the assumptions behind them, and a way to check later whether it was right.

Simple methods and when they fit
MethodExcelWorks when
Trend lineFORECAST, SLOPESteady growth or decline, no strong seasons
Seasonal naiveSame period last year × growth factorA strong yearly pattern
Moving averageAVERAGE of the last few valuesA level series with noise, short-term
Trend × seasonal indexFORECAST × indexA trend and a repeating pattern
Worked example

A forecast with a range

A trend line predicts 5.8 for next month. The last six months differed from the line by up to about 0.8.

  1. Central forecast: 5.8.
  2. Plausible range: 5.8 ± 0.8, so 5.0 to 6.6.
  3. Plan stock for the middle, with a buffer to reach the top of the range.

Answer. A range tells decision makers how much to rely on the number, and what to prepare for.

How to measure a forecast's error

  • Error = actual − forecast, for each period.
  • Mean absolute error: the average of the errors ignoring sign, =AVERAGE(ABS errors). In the same units as the data.
  • Percentage error: error ÷ actual, easier to compare between products. Watch out for actuals near zero.
Watch out

Forecasts fail when the world changes: a new competitor, a price change, a festival moving dates, a pandemic. State the assumptions ('no price change, normal season') so the reader knows when to distrust it.

Common mistakes

  • Giving one exact forecast.
  • Fitting a complicated method to 12 data points.
  • Never comparing forecasts with what actually happened.
Try it yourself: Why is a range better than one number?

Model answer. It shows the uncertainty, so people can plan for the worse and the better cases.

Check what you just learned

1. A good forecast gives:
  • One exact number
  • A central estimate, a range and the assumptions (correct)
  • Only a chart
  • A guess

Uncertainty must be visible.

2. Mean absolute error is:
  • The average of signed errors
  • The largest error
  • The average of errors ignoring sign (correct)
  • The sum of forecasts

It avoids positives and negatives cancelling out.

Key terms: flip and sort

Correlation (r)
Strength of a straight-line link from −1 to +1.
R squared
Share of variation a line explains.
Slope
Change in y per unit of x.
Confounder
A hidden factor driving two things at once.
Moving average
The average of the latest few periods.
Seasonal index
A period's value divided by the overall average.
Extrapolation
Predicting outside the range of the data.
keyPoints: A forecast is a range with stated assumptions.
Start with simple methods; measure the error against actuals.
Revisit forecasts and improve them.

modules.title: Models, scenarios and decisions
modules.summary: Build what-if models, test assumptions, run an A/B test with a significance check, and compare options with a weighted score and expected value.
modules.outcome: You can structure a model with inputs and assumptions, compute break-even and scenarios, test whether a difference between two rates is likely to be real, and compare options transparently.
modules.intro: Analysis exists to support decisions: launch or wait, option A or B, keep or cut. This module turns your Excel skills into decision tools. You build models where changing an assumption updates the answer, you test whether a difference you see is large enough to trust, and you compare options with explicit criteria rather than gut feeling.

topics.title: What-if models: inputs, assumptions and outputs
topics.html:
A good spreadsheet model has three zones: inputs (assumptions you can change), calculations (formulas that use the inputs) and outputs (the answers). Keeping them separate lets anyone change an assumption and see the result, and lets a reviewer audit the logic.

Model layout
ZoneContainsConvention
InputsPrices, costs, growth rates, unitsOne cell each, clearly labelled, in a marked colour
CalculationsFormulas onlyNever type numbers inside formulas; refer to input cells
OutputsProfit, break-even, marginAt the top or on a summary, linked to the calculations
Worked example

A simple profit model

A product sells for ₹500 and costs ₹300 to make. Fixed costs are ₹200,000 a year.

  1. Contribution per unit = price − variable cost = ₹200.
  2. Profit = units × contribution − fixed costs.
  3. At 1,200 units: 1,200 × 200 − 200,000 = ₹40,000.

Answer. Because each number lives in its own input cell, changing the price to ₹550 instantly updates every result.

Formula · Profit

profit = units × (price − variable cost) − fixed costs

Every term is an input cell, so no number is buried inside a formula.

Rules for trustworthy models

  • No hard-coded numbers in formulas: =B2*B3 not =B2*0.18; put 0.18 in an input cell.
  • One calculation, one place: do not repeat the same logic in several cells.
  • Label units: rupees, thousands, per month.
  • Check totals: the model should reconcile to a known figure.
  • Document assumptions: where each input came from.
Watch out

Hard-coded numbers are the leading cause of spreadsheet errors. When a price changes, the model silently keeps using the old one in the formulas you forgot.

Common mistakes

  • Typing assumptions into formulas.
  • Mixing inputs and outputs so nobody knows what to change.
  • Building one huge formula that nobody can check.
Try it yourself: Write the formula for profit if price is in B1, variable cost in B2, fixed cost in B3 and units in B4.

Model answer. =B4*(B1-B2)-B3

Check what you just learned

1. Where should a tax rate used in many formulas be stored?
  • Typed in every formula
  • In the title
  • In a comment
  • In one labelled input cell (correct)

One place makes it easy to change and audit.

2. The three zones of a model are:
  • Inputs, calculations and outputs (correct)
  • Rows, columns and cells
  • Charts, tables and pivots
  • Text, numbers and dates

Keep them distinct.
keyPoints: Separate inputs, calculations and outputs.
Never hard-code assumptions inside formulas.
Document, label and reconcile.

topics.title: Break-even and scenarios
topics.html:
Break-even is the volume at which profit is zero. Scenarios (worst, base, best) show how the result moves when several assumptions change together.

Formula · Break-even units

break-even = fixed costs ÷ (price − variable cost)

In the example: 200,000 ÷ 200 = 1,000 units.

Three scenarios for the ₹500 product (fixed cost ₹200,000, unit contribution ₹200)
ScenarioUnitsProfit
Worst800−₹40,000
Base1,200₹40,000
Best1,600₹120,000

Break-even and profit

Change the price, cost and volume. The result updates, and the margin of safety shows how far volume can fall before you lose money.

Adjust Price per unit, Variable cost per unit, Fixed costs per year, Units sold and see Break-even units, Profit, Margin of safety (volume above break-even) change.

Worked example

Margin of safety

Base case: 1,200 units against a break-even of 1,000.

  1. Volume above break-even = 200 units.
  2. Margin of safety = 200 ÷ 1,200 = 16.7%.
  3. Sales could fall by about a sixth before the product starts to lose money.

Answer. It turns 'we make a profit' into 'we can survive a 16.7% drop'.

Scenarios are best built with a scenario selector: a cell holding 1, 2 or 3, and the function CHOOSE(selector, worst, base, best) to pick the matching assumption. Change the selector and the whole model switches.

Watch out

Scenarios are not forecasts: they are 'what if' stories. Choose them to answer a question (can we survive a bad year?), and say what each assumes.

Common mistakes

  • A best case that is just the base plus 10% with no reason.
  • Changing many assumptions at once and not knowing which mattered.
  • Forgetting that costs often change with volume.
Try it yourself: What is the break-even with fixed costs of 300,000 and contribution of 150 per unit?

Model answer. 300,000 ÷ 150 = 2,000 units.

Check what you just learned

1. Break-even units equal:
  • Price × units
  • Fixed costs ÷ (price − variable cost) (correct)
  • Variable cost × units
  • Profit ÷ price

Each unit contributes price − variable cost toward fixed costs.

2. CHOOSE(2, a, b, c) returns:
  • a
  • c
  • b (correct)
  • 2

The second value.
keyPoints: Break-even = fixed costs ÷ unit contribution.
Margin of safety shows how far volume can fall.
Use a scenario selector with CHOOSE to switch assumptions.

topics.title: A/B tests: is the difference real?
topics.html:
Two versions of a page convert at 5.0% and 6.0%. Is version B really better, or did it just get lucky? Chance alone makes rates wobble, especially with few visitors. An A/B test with a significance check asks: if there were really no difference, how likely is a gap this big?

The test data
VersionVisitorsConversionsRate
A2,4001205.0%
B2,5001506.0%
Formula · The calculation

z = (pB − pA) ÷ √( p(1 − p) × (1/nA + 1/nB) )

p is the pooled rate. Two-sided p-value: =2*(1-NORM.S.DIST(ABS(z),TRUE)).

Worked example

Working it through

With the table above:

  1. Pooled rate = 270 ÷ 4,900 = 0.0551.
  2. Standard error = √(0.0551 × 0.9449 × (1/2,400 + 1/2,500)) = 0.00652.
  3. z = 0.01 ÷ 0.00652 = 1.53.
  4. p-value = 2 × (1 − NORM.S.DIST(1.53)) = 0.125.

Answer. A p-value of 0.125 means that if the versions were truly equal, a gap this large would happen about 1 time in 8 by chance. That is not strong enough to claim B is better at the usual 5% threshold.

How sample size changes the evidence

Keep the rates at 5% and 6%. See how the evidence (z) grows with the number of visitors in each group.

Adjust Visitors in each version and see z (about 1.96 or more is significant at 5%), Evidence needed (z at 5%) change.

Watch out

Significant is not the same as important, and not significant is not the same as no effect. A huge test can find a tiny difference significant that is worthless in practice. A small test can miss a real, valuable gain. Report the size of the difference as well as the p-value.

Rules for fair tests

  • Decide the sample size and the metric before you start.
  • Do not stop early the moment the result looks good: it inflates false positives.
  • Randomly assign visitors to versions.
  • Test one change at a time.
  • Run through full weekly cycles.

Common mistakes

  • Declaring a winner after a few hundred visitors.
  • Checking the p-value daily and stopping when it dips below 0.05.
  • Treating p = 0.06 as 'nothing' and p = 0.04 as 'proof'.
Try it yourself: A test gives p = 0.30. What can you say?

Model answer. The difference could easily be chance: the data does not show B is better. It does not prove they are equal; you may need more data.

Check what you just learned

1. A p-value of 0.125 means:
  • B is better with 87.5% certainty
  • The versions are equal
  • The test failed
  • A gap this large would occur about 12.5% of the time by chance alone (correct)

It is the probability of such a gap under no real difference.

2. Why not stop a test as soon as p < 0.05?
  • Peeking inflates false positives (correct)
  • It is illegal
  • Excel crashes
  • It makes z negative

Repeated checks make a chance result likely to appear significant.
keyPoints: An A/B test compares rates and asks how likely the gap is by chance.
z = difference ÷ standard error; p-value from NORM.S.DIST.
Report effect size, not only significance; fix the sample size in advance.

topics.title: Choosing between options: scores and expected value
topics.html:
When a decision has several criteria (cost, quality, speed), a weighted score makes the trade-offs explicit. Agree the criteria and weights first, score each option, and multiply. The calculation is SUMPRODUCT(weights, scores).

Choosing a supplier
OptionCost (40%)Quality (35%)Speed (25%)Weighted score
A7867.10
B9677.45
C6997.80

Option C wins, although it is the weakest on cost. The weights, not the arithmetic, decide: with a cost weight of 70%, the answer would change. So test it: change the weights and see if the ranking holds. If it does, the decision is robust.

Formula · Expected value

EV = Σ (probability × payoff)

Use it for choices with uncertain results: 60% chance of +₹100,000 and a 40% chance of −₹50,000 gives 0.6 × 100,000 + 0.4 × (−50,000) = ₹40,000.

Worked example

Is the risky project worth it?

A project returns ₹100,000 with 60% probability and loses ₹50,000 with 40%. A safe alternative returns ₹30,000 for certain.

  1. EV of the project = ₹40,000.
  2. Safe option = ₹30,000.
  3. The project has the higher average, but a 40% chance of losing money.

Answer. If you can afford a loss and will make many such bets, take the higher EV. If one loss would hurt badly, the safe option may still be wiser. Numbers inform; they do not decide.

Watch out

Weights and probabilities are estimates. Do not present 7.80 vs 7.45 as precise. Show how the answer changes under different assumptions, and be clear about what is a judgement.

Common mistakes

  • Weights that do not add up to 100%.
  • Criteria that overlap, so one factor is counted twice.
  • Believing the score removes the need for judgement.
Try it yourself: What is the weighted score of an option scoring 5, 8 and 7 on criteria weighted 50%, 30% and 20%?

Model answer. 0.5 × 5 + 0.3 × 8 + 0.2 × 7 = 2.5 + 2.4 + 1.4 = 6.3.

Check what you just learned

1. Weights in a weighted score should:
  • Be random
  • Add up to 100% (correct)
  • Be equal
  • Be negative

They represent shares of importance.

2. Expected value of a 50% chance of 100 and a 50% chance of −20 is:
  • −20
  • 80
  • 40 (correct)
  • 100

0.5 × 100 + 0.5 × (−20) = 40.

Key terms: flip and sort

Input
An assumption you can change.
Break-even
The volume at which profit is zero.
Margin of safety
How far volume can fall before a loss.
Scenario
A named set of assumptions.
p-value
How often a gap this big would occur by chance if there were no real difference.
Expected value
The probability-weighted average payoff.
Weighted score
Scores multiplied by importance weights.
keyPoints: A weighted score makes trade-offs explicit; test the weights for robustness.
Expected value = sum of probability × payoff.
Numbers support decisions; judgement and risk tolerance remain.

modules.title: Dashboards, charts and storytelling
modules.summary: Design a one-screen dashboard of KPIs, choose honest charts, make a workbook robust, and present findings so people act on them.
modules.outcome: You can pick the right KPIs and charts, avoid misleading visuals, structure a robust workbook, and write a finding that leads with the answer and ends with an action.
modules.intro: An analysis nobody understands changes nothing. This last module is about turning numbers into something a busy person can read in five seconds and act on. You design a KPI dashboard, choose charts that tell the truth, make the workbook hold together when data changes, and learn the shape of a good data story. The desktop tools (conditional formatting, slicers, Power BI) are mentioned where they help, and the thinking carries to all of them.

topics.title: KPIs and dashboard design
topics.html:
A KPI (key performance indicator) is a measure tied to a goal, with a target and a time period. A dashboard is a single screen of the few KPIs that decide whether things are on track, not everything you can measure.

A good KPI is

  • Linked to a goal: it moves when the goal is achieved.
  • Defined: everyone computes it the same way (what counts as an 'active customer'?).
  • Compared: against a target, last period or last year, because a number alone has no meaning.
  • Actionable: someone can do something when it moves.
  • Few: five to seven on one screen.
A KPI card in formulas
ElementFormula or content
Value=SUM(Revenue) for the month
TargetAn input cell
% of target=value / target
Status=IF(pct>=1,"On track",IF(pct>=0.9,"Watch","Behind"))
TrendThis month vs last month: =value - previous
Worked example

The five-second test

A manager opens the dashboard.

  1. Can they say within five seconds whether things are good or bad? Use clear status words and a few strong colours.
  2. Can they see what changed? Put the comparison next to the number.
  3. Can they find the cause? Offer one level of detail below the headline.

Answer. If the answer to any is no, remove something rather than add more.

Watch out

Vanity metrics make a dashboard feel good without helping decisions: total page views, total sign-ups since the beginning of time. Prefer rates, comparisons and measures that connect to money or goals.

Tip

Put the most important number at the top left, because that is where people look first. Group related KPIs. Leave white space.

Common mistakes

  • Thirty charts on one sheet.
  • A KPI with no target or comparison.
  • Different definitions of the same KPI in different places.
Try it yourself: Revenue is 92,000 against a target of 100,000. What is the % of target and a suitable status?

Model answer. 92%: 'Watch' (between 90% and 100%) using the status rule above.

Check what you just learned

1. A number with no target or comparison is:
  • A KPI
  • A dashboard
  • A chart
  • Hard to interpret (correct)

Meaning comes from comparison.

2. How many KPIs belong on one dashboard screen?
  • Five to seven (correct)
  • Fifty
  • One hundred
  • None

Few, so they can be read at a glance.
keyPoints: A KPI links to a goal, is defined, compared with a target, and actionable.
A dashboard shows five to seven KPIs that can be read in five seconds.
Prefer rates and comparisons over vanity totals.

topics.title: Choosing honest charts
topics.html:
The right chart depends on the question. The wrong one hides the answer or, worse, creates a false impression.

Question to chart
You want to showUseAvoid
Compare categoriesHorizontal or vertical bars, sortedPie charts with many slices
Change over timeA line chartA bar chart with a truncated axis
Parts of a whole (few parts)A single stacked bar or a pie with 2 to 4 slices3D pies
Relationship between two numbersA scatter plotTwo separate bar charts
DistributionA histogramAn average alone
A single KPI against a targetA big number with a statusA decorative gauge

Rules that keep a chart honest

  • Bars start at zero. A truncated bar makes a small difference look large.
  • Label the axes and units, and write a title that states the finding ('East grew faster than North').
  • Sort categories by value unless there is a natural order.
  • Use colour sparingly: one colour for the thing you want noticed, grey for the rest.
  • Do not use 3D, shadows or decoration. They add no information.
  • One message per chart.
Watch out

A line chart may start above zero, because it shows change, but a bar chart must not. Changing the axis to exaggerate a trend is one of the most common ways charts mislead.

Worked example

Fixing a misleading chart

A bar chart of monthly sales shows 98 and 100 with the vertical axis starting at 96. The second bar looks double the first.

  1. Start the axis at 0 so the bars show their true proportions.
  2. Or switch to a line chart if the point is the change over time.
  3. Add the data labels so nobody needs to estimate.

Answer. The honest chart shows a 2% difference, which is what it is.

Common mistakes

  • A pie with eight slices.
  • Using red and green only, which some viewers cannot tell apart.
  • Charts with no title or units.
Try it yourself: Which chart suits 'sales by month for the last two years'?

Model answer. A line chart, with one line per year, so the viewer sees the trend and compares the same months.

Check what you just learned

1. Which chart type suits change over time?
  • Pie
  • Line (correct)
  • 3D bar
  • Scatter without labels

A line shows trends.

2. A bar chart whose axis starts at 96 will:
  • Be fine
  • Hide data
  • Exaggerate differences (correct)
  • Be a line

Bar length should be proportional to the value.
keyPoints: Choose the chart from the question: bars to compare, lines for time, scatter for relationships, histogram for distribution.
Bars start at zero; label axes; title with the finding.
Remove decoration and use colour to emphasise.

topics.title: Making a workbook robust
topics.html:
A dashboard that breaks when the data grows, or that only its author understands, is a liability. A few features make a workbook last.

Features that make workbooks robust
FeatureWhat it does
Excel Tables (Ctrl+T)A named range that grows automatically; formulas use readable names such as Sales[Revenue]
Named rangesA label for a cell or range, so =Profit replaces =Model!$B$14
Data validationRestricts what can be typed in a cell: a list, a number range, a date
Conditional formattingColours cells by rule: red when behind target
Freeze panes and sheet protectionKeep headers visible and stop accidental overwriting of formulas
Error checkingIFERROR for expected errors; ISNUMBER checks for text-numbers
Documentation sheetA 'README' sheet explaining the purpose, sources, assumptions and how to refresh
Worked example

Why Tables beat plain ranges

A report uses =SUM(B2:B501) over 500 rows. Next month there are 520 rows.

  1. The formula still sums only 500 rows: 20 rows are silently missed.
  2. With an Excel Table named Sales, =SUM(Sales[Revenue]) always covers every row, however many are added.
  3. Charts and pivots based on the Table also grow.

Answer. Convert data to a Table before building anything on it.

Watch out

IFERROR can hide real mistakes. Use it for errors you expect (a zero denominator), not to silence everything. A dashboard full of dashes may be hiding broken formulas.

A pre-flight checklist before sharing

  • Totals reconcile to the source.
  • No error values, no hard-coded numbers inside formulas.
  • Inputs are marked and labelled; assumptions documented.
  • Sheet names, headings and units are clear.
  • Cells you do not want edited are protected.
  • Someone else has tried to use it.

Common mistakes

  • Referencing fixed ranges that miss new rows.
  • Colouring cells by hand instead of conditional rules.
  • Leaving calculation errors hidden under IFERROR.

Check what you just learned

1. Why convert data to an Excel Table?
  • It looks nicer
  • It deletes blanks
  • It prevents sorting
  • Formulas and charts grow automatically as rows are added (correct)

Table references expand.

2. Data validation is used to:
  • Limit what can be typed into a cell (correct)
  • Chart data
  • Format dates
  • Sum values

It restricts input.
keyPoints: Tables and named ranges make formulas grow with the data and read clearly.
Validation and protection prevent accidents; IFERROR is for expected errors only.
Document, reconcile and test with another person before sharing.

topics.title: Telling the story: from finding to action
topics.html:
People remember stories and forget tables. A data story does not walk through your analysis in the order you did it; it leads with the answer.

Weak and strong headlines
Weak (a topic)Strong (a finding)
Sales by regionEast grew twice as fast as North, but is still the smallest region
Customer survey resultsDelivery time, not price, is the main reason customers leave
Q3 performanceWe are 8% behind target, and the gap is entirely in one product line
Worked example

A one-paragraph finding

A manager asks why revenue fell.

  1. Headline: Revenue fell 12% in March because of one lost customer.
  2. Evidence: that customer was 14% of February revenue; without them, revenue rose 2%.
  3. Limit: we have only two months of data, so we cannot say whether others will follow.
  4. Recommendation: contact the five customers with the most similar order pattern this week.

Answer. In four sentences the reader knows the answer, why to believe it, how far to trust it, and what to do.

Writing for a busy reader

  • Put the conclusion first.
  • Use plain words; define a metric the first time.
  • One idea per paragraph, one message per chart.
  • Show the number and the comparison together.
  • Say what you do not know.
Watch out

Never hide a limit that changes the conclusion. If the answer depends on an assumption, say so. Credibility, once lost, is hard to get back.

Common mistakes

  • Starting with the method instead of the answer.
  • A recommendation that is not specific (who, what, by when).
  • Overclaiming certainty.
Try it yourself: Rewrite 'Customer churn analysis' as a strong headline given that churn is highest in the first month.

Model answer. 'Most customers who leave do so in their first month, so onboarding is where to improve retention.'

Check what you just learned

1. A strong report headline:
  • Names the topic
  • States the finding (correct)
  • Lists the methods
  • Is a question

Readers want the answer first.

2. Which should always appear in a data story?
  • Every formula
  • The author's name
  • The limits of the data (correct)
  • Colour codes

Honesty about limits builds trust.

Key terms: flip and sort

KPI
A measure linked to a goal, with a target.
Vanity metric
A number that looks good but drives no decision.
Excel Table
A named range that grows with the data.
Data validation
A rule limiting what can be entered.
Conditional formatting
Colour applied by rule.
Headline
The finding, stated in one sentence.
keyPoints: Lead with the answer; follow with evidence, limits and a recommendation.
Strong headlines state a finding, not a topic.
Be specific about the action and honest about the limits.
